claim: The striatum serves an important role in motor control.
source: The striatum serves an important role in motor control, and neurons in this area encode the body's initiation, cessation, and speed of locomotion.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Striatal neurons encode the body's initiation, cessation, and speed of locomotion.
source: The striatum serves an important role in motor control, and neurons in this area encode the body's initiation, cessation, and speed of locomotion.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: A sizable population of both D1 and D2 receptor expressing medium spiny projection neurons (MSNs) were phase-locked to the gait cycle of individual limbs in mice.
source: By combining high-speed video tracking, electrophysiology, and optogenetic tagging, we found that a sizable population of both D1 and D2 receptor expressing medium spiny projection neurons (MSNs) were phase-locked to the gait cycle of individual limbs in mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from electrophysiology and optogenetic tagging experiments.

claim: Healthy animals showed balanced limb phase-locking between D1 and D2 MSNs.
source: Healthy animals showed balanced limb phase-locking between D1 and D2 MSNs, while dopamine depletion led to stronger phase-locking in D2 MSNs.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data comparing D1 and D2 MSN activity in healthy animals.

claim: Dopamine depletion led to stronger phase-locking in D2 MSNs.
source: Healthy animals showed balanced limb phase-locking between D1 and D2 MSNs, while dopamine depletion led to stronger phase-locking in D2 MSNs.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from dopamine-lesioned animals.

claim: Striatal neurons represent gait on a single-limb and step basis.
source: These findings indicate that striatal neurons represent gait on a single-limb and step basis, and suggest that elevated limb phase-locking of D2 MSNs may underlie some of the gait impairments associated with dopamine loss.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Elevated limb phase-locking of D2 MSNs may underlie some of the gait impairments associated with dopamine loss.
source: These findings indicate that striatal neurons represent gait on a single-limb and step basis, and suggest that elevated limb phase-locking of D2 MSNs may underlie some of the gait impairments associated with dopamine loss.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Spinal cord microcircuits are ultimately responsible for producing limb movements.
source: While spinal cord microcircuits are ultimately responsible for producing limb movements, the voluntary control of walking is thought to rely on sensorimotor signals from multiple cortical and subcortical areas, including the basal ganglia (Arber and Costa, 2022; Takakusaki, 2013; Roseberry et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: The voluntary control of walking is thought to rely on sensorimotor signals from multiple cortical and subcortical areas, including the basal ganglia.
source: While spinal cord microcircuits are ultimately responsible for producing limb movements, the voluntary control of walking is thought to rely on sensorimotor signals from multiple cortical and subcortical areas, including the basal ganglia (Arber and Costa, 2022; Takakusaki, 2013; Roseberry et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Altered signaling in the direct and indirect pathways of the basal ganglia is implicated in the motor symptoms of movement disorders such as Parkinson's disease.
source: A large body of work has examined the role of the direct and indirect pathways of the basal ganglia in locomotion, as altered signaling in these circuits is implicated in the motor symptoms of movement disorders such as Parkinson's disease (Albin et al., 1989; DeLong, 1990; Kravitz et al., 2010; Parker et al., 2018; Maltese et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: D1 and D2 MSNs in the striatum have been shown to represent both discrete aspects of locomotion such as the initiation and cessation of movement, as well as continuous aspects such as body speed.
source: These pathways, originating in D1 and D2 MSNs in the striatum, have been shown to represent both discrete aspects of locomotion such as the initiation and cessation of movement, as well as continuous aspects such as body speed (DeLong, 1972; Jin and Costa, 2010; Fobbs et al., 2020; Rueda-Orozco and Robbe, 2015; Jog et al., 1999; Barbera et al., 2016; Schultz and Romo, 1988).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Most studies of striatal activity during locomotion have relied on relatively low spatial resolution measures of motion.
source: Yet, with few exceptions (Dhawale et al., 2021; Markowitz et al., 2018), most of these studies have relied on relatively low spatial resolution measures of motion – whole-body movements – to link striatal activity specifically to locomotor function (work has examined other types of limb movements, such as lever pressing, but this is a behaviorally distinct process from gait Panigrahi et al., 2015; Oldenburg and Sabatini, 2015).
evidence: This is a characterization of prior research with supporting citations.

claim: There has been little effort to link D1 and D2 MSN activity to gait with single-limb and step resolution.
source: Thus, despite significant conceptual advances, there has been little effort to link D1 and D2 MSN activity to gait with single-limb and step resolution.
evidence: This is a characterization of the gap in prior research.

claim: Dopamine degeneration in Parkinson's disease is associated with impaired gait.
source: Dopamine degeneration in Parkinson's disease is associated with impaired gait, but the neural mechanisms underlying many of these behavioral changes are unclear (Mirelman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: The neural mechanisms underlying gait impairments in Parkinson's disease are unclear.
source: Dopamine degeneration in Parkinson's disease is associated with impaired gait, but the neural mechanisms underlying many of these behavioral changes are unclear (Mirelman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Mice walked with a lateral sequence gait pattern (LR→LF→RR→RF), with the limbs on the same side of the body moving first.
source: Mice walked with a lateral sequence gait pattern (LR→LF→RR→RF), with the limbs on the same side of the body moving first (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The front and rear limbs on the same side of the body moved with an approximately anti-phase relationship (180° phase offset).
source: Furthermore, the front and rear limbs on the same side of the body moved with an approximately anti-phase relationship (180° phase offset, Figure 1F; Machado et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis supported by data shown in Figure 1F and a citation.

claim: Faster strides are associated with higher length and frequency.
source: We next characterized the properties of individual limb strides, and confirmed that faster strides are associated with higher length and frequency (Figure 1G and H; Machado et al., 2015), and that whole-body speed is strongly correlated with stride speed (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis supported by data shown in Figures 1G and 1H and a citation.

claim: Whole-body speed is strongly correlated with stride speed.
source: We next characterized the properties of individual limb strides, and confirmed that faster strides are associated with higher length and frequency (Figure 1G and H; Machado et al., 2015), and that whole-body speed is strongly correlated with stride speed (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis supported by data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Stride parameters in healthy mice appeared normally distributed and were similar across the four limbs.
source: Stride parameters in healthy mice appeared normally distributed and were similar across the four limbs (Figure 1J–L).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis supported by data shown in Figures 1J-L.

claim: Around 45% of striatal neurons showed significant phase-locking to at least one limb.
source: In total, around 45% of striatal neurons (total includes all cell types) showed significant phase-locking to at least one limb, which was determined via a spike time jitter test (see Methods; Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the electrophysiology analysis supported by data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: There was no significant difference in mean vector length across the four limbs.
source: There was no significant difference in mean vector length across the four limbs (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiology analysis supported by data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The mean spike-limb phase angle distribution was similar for diagonal limbs, and offset by approximately 180° for off-diagonal limbs.
source: Consistent with the relative phase of limb motion, the mean spike-limb phase angle distribution was similar for diagonal limbs, and offset by approximately 180° for off-diagonal limbs (Figure 2J and K).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiology analysis supported by data shown in Figures 2J and 2K.

claim: The majority of phase-locked neurons were entrained to either a single limb or pair of limbs.
source: The majority of phase-locked neurons were entrained to either a single limb or pair of limbs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiology analysis supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Among the cells that were coupled to only two limbs, most of the limb pairs were diagonal.
source: Among the cells that were coupled to only two limbs, most of the limb pairs were diagonal (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiology analysis supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There was a significant bias in the mean vector length when ranked based on the single limb preference, ranging from the highest to the lowest.
source: We also observed a significant bias in the mean vector length when ranked based on the single limb preference, ranging from the highest to the lowest (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiology analysis supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: On average the vector length did not show a bias for either ipsi- or contra-lateral limbs.
source: While single-limb phase-locking was widespread, on average the vector length did not show a bias for either ipsi- or contra-lateral limbs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiology analysis supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The vector length was negatively correlated with a neuron's firing rate averaged across the entire recording session.
source: Finally, the vector length was negatively correlated with a neuron's firing rate averaged across the entire recording session, while it did not consistently vary along the depth of the dorsal striatum (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiology analysis supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The vector length did not consistently vary along the depth of the dorsal striatum.
source: Finally, the vector length was negatively correlated with a neuron's firing rate averaged across the entire recording session, while it did not consistently vary along the depth of the dorsal striatum (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiology analysis supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: A substantial proportion of dorsal striatal neurons exhibited significant modulation to single-limb phase, body speed and/or the initiation and cessation of movement.
source: This suggests that the striatum may contain a mixed representation of both single-limb and whole-body movements related to walking. Consistent with this assumption, our analysis indicated that a substantial proportion of dorsal striatal neurons exhibited significant modulation to single-limb phase, body speed and/or the initiation and cessation of movement (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiology analysis supported by data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Around one third of striatal neurons encoded all three factors (limb phase, body speed, and movement initiation/cessation).
source: Notably, around one third of striatal neurons encoded all three factors (Figure 3C–G).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiology analysis supported by data shown in Figures 3C-G.

claim: D1 and D2 MSNs were identified via an optogenetic tagging protocol.
source: D1 and D2 MSNs were identified via an optogenetic tagging protocol performed at the conclusion of each recording session.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: 39 D1 and 40 D2 MSNs were identified in healthy mice.
source: In total, we identified 39 D1 and 40 D2 MSNs in healthy mice, with a statistically similar average session-wide firing rate (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a finding from the optogenetic tagging experiments supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: D1 and D2 MSNs in healthy mice had a statistically similar average session-wide firing rate.
source: In total, we identified 39 D1 and 40 D2 MSNs in healthy mice, with a statistically similar average session-wide firing rate (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a finding from the optogenetic tagging experiments supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Across all identified cells there was no significant difference between D1 and D2 MSNs in either the mean vector length or angle.
source: Across all identified cells there was no significant difference between D1 and D2 MSNs in either the mean vector length or angle (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is a finding from the optogenetic tagging experiments supported by data shown in Figures 4F and 4G.

claim: There is normally a balanced level of D1 and D2 MSN activity coupled to the gait cycle.
source: These results suggest that there is normally a balanced level of D1 and D2 MSN activity coupled to the gait cycle.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Both D1 and D2 MSN populations showed a similar proportion of neurons which encoded limb phase, start of movement, body speed, and the combination of these.
source: Furthermore, both populations showed a similar proportion of neurons which encoded limb phase, start of movement, body speed, and the combination of these (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a finding from the optogenetic tagging experiments supported by data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: D1 and D2 MSNs both increase their activity around the time of movement initiation.
source: Previous work has shown that D1 and D2 MSNs both increase their activity around the time of movement initiation (Barbera et al., 2016; Cui et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: The fractional change in start-related activity was significantly higher in D1 MSNs compared to D2 MSNs.
source: In line with these findings, on average we observed an elevated firing rate in both populations during the start of whole-body motion; however, the fractional change in start-related activity was significantly higher in D1 MSNs (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is a finding from the optogenetic tagging experiments supported by data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Neural responses to movement cessation and speed were similar between D1 and D2 MSNs.
source: Neural responses to movement cessation and speed were similar between D1 and D2 MSNs (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is a finding from the optogenetic tagging experiments supported by data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: In healthy animals, D1 and D2 MSNs exhibit similar levels of activity while locomotion is in progress, but there is an initial bias toward the direct pathway at the start of movement.
source: Our data indicate that, in healthy animals, D1 and D2 MSNs exhibit similar levels of activity while locomotion is in progress, but that there is an initial bias toward the direct pathway at the start of movement.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Unilateral 6OHDA injections into the medial forebrain bundle led to loss of dopamine in the dorsal striatum.
source: In a separate group of animals, we administered unilateral 6-hydroxydopamine (6OHDA) injections into the medial forebrain bundle, leading to loss of dopamine in the dorsal striatum (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation and its effect, supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Dopamine lesions led to impaired locomotion measured at the whole-body level.
source: We first confirmed that dopamine lesions led to impaired locomotion measured at the whole-body level (Figure 5A–F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C; Kravitz et al., 2010; Ungerstedt and Arbuthnott, 1970).
evidence: This is a finding from the dopamine lesion experiments supported by data shown in Figures 5A-F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C, and citations.

claim: Walking bouts in 6OHDA-injected animals were characterized by frequent ipsiversive turning, lower body speed, shorter overall distance traveled, and a lower rate of initiating locomotion.
source: Walking bouts in 6OHDA-injected animals were characterized by frequent ipsiversive turning, lower body speed, shorter overall distance traveled, and a lower rate of initiating locomotion.
evidence: This is a finding from the dopamine lesion experiments.

claim: Dopamine-lesioned animals displayed significant changes in stride length and duration, leading to slower strides for each of the four limbs.
source: These deficits in whole-body motion were accompanied by changes in gait performance at the individual limb level. Dopamine-lesioned animals displayed significant changes in stride length and duration, leading to slower strides for each of the four limbs (Figure 5G–I; Hsieh et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a finding from the dopamine lesion experiments supported by data shown in Figures 5G-I and a citation.

claim: Dopamine-lesioned animals showed a shorter swing-to-stance duration ratio, indicating that during walking each limb spent more time in contact with the ground.
source: We further observed a shorter swing-to-stance duration ratio, indicating that during walking each limb spent more time in contact with the ground (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is a finding from the dopamine lesion experiments supported by data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Additional changes in gait after dopamine lesions included lower coordination between different pairs of limbs, and higher variability in the length and speed of individual strides.
source: Additional changes in gait included lower coordination between different pairs of limbs, and higher variability in the length and speed of individual strides (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–H).
evidence: This is a finding from the dopamine lesion experiments supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-H.

claim: Dopamine lesions impair multiple aspects of locomotion, notably both the ability to initiate movement and, once walking is underway, to perform rapid, sustained, and coordinated limb movements that are typical of a healthy gait pattern.
source: Overall, it was evident that dopamine lesions impair multiple aspects of locomotion, notably both the ability to initiate movement and, once walking is underway, to perform rapid, sustained, and coordinated limb movements that are typical of a healthy gait pattern.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings from dopamine lesion experiments.

claim: Sham-lesioned animals displayed similar D1 and D2 MSN limb phase-locking properties measured across the four limbs.
source: We confirmed that, as in healthy mice, sham-lesioned animals displayed similar D1 and D2 MSN limb phase-locking properties measured across the four limbs (Figure 6A–C), and a similar mean level of firing across the recording session (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a finding from the sham-lesion control experiments supported by data shown in Figures 6A-C.

claim: Sham-lesioned animals showed a similar mean level of D1 and D2 MSN firing across the recording session.
source: We confirmed that, as in healthy mice, sham-lesioned animals displayed similar D1 and D2 MSN limb phase-locking properties measured across the four limbs (Figure 6A–C), and a similar mean level of firing across the recording session (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a finding from the sham-lesion control experiments supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The balanced phase-locking activity between D1 and D2 MSNs was disrupted in 6OHDA-lesioned animals, which exhibited a significantly higher average spike-limb phase vector length among the D2 MSN population.
source: However, this originally balanced phase-locking activity was disrupted in 6OHDA-lesioned animals, which exhibited a significantly higher average spike-limb phase vector length among the D2 MSN population (Figure 6E and F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the dopamine lesion experiments supported by data shown in Figures 6E, 6F, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The average vector angle remained similar between D1 and D2 MSNs in the 6OHDA group.
source: The average vector angle remained similar between the two MSN subtypes in the 6OHDA group (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a finding from the dopamine lesion experiments supported by data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Dopamine lesions strengthen the coupling of D2 MSNs to the gait cycle, whereas the coupling of D1 MSNs is unaltered.
source: Thus, dopamine lesions strengthen the coupling of D2 MSNs to the gait cycle, whereas the coupling of D1 MSNs is unaltered.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings from dopamine lesion experiments.

claim: The session-wide firing rate between D1 and D2 MSNs remained statistically similar after dopamine lesions.
source: However, the session-wide firing rate between D1 and D2 MSNs remained statistically similar (Figure 6H), suggesting that the observed imbalance in vector length cannot be explained by changes in overall firing rate.
evidence: This is a finding from the dopamine lesion experiments supported by data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: The observed imbalance in vector length after dopamine lesions cannot be explained by changes in overall firing rate.
source: However, the session-wide firing rate between D1 and D2 MSNs remained statistically similar (Figure 6H), suggesting that the observed imbalance in vector length cannot be explained by changes in overall firing rate.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Healthy mice exhibited significantly higher D1 MSN activity during movement initiation relative to D2 MSNs.
source: Since healthy mice exhibited significantly higher D1 MSN activity during movement initiation, we confirmed the same observation in sham-lesioned mice (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments supported by data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Dopamine lesions attenuated the bias toward higher D1 MSN activity during movement initiation, with both MSN subtypes now showing similar levels of start-related activity.
source: In contrast, dopamine lesions attenuated this bias, with both MSN subtypes now showing similar levels of start-related activity (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is a finding from the dopamine lesion experiments supported by data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: Neither the encoding of movement cessation nor body speed showed a significant difference between D1 and D2 MSNs in the sham and 6OHDA groups.
source: Neither the encoding of movement cessation nor body speed showed a significant difference between D1 and D2 MSNs in the sham and 6OHDA groups (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-E.

claim: There was a substantial reduction in the speed coding score of both D1 and D2 MSN cell types after dopamine lesions.
source: However, while speed coding remained balanced between D1 and D2 MSNs, there was a substantial reduction in the speed coding score of both cell types after dopamine lesions.
evidence: This is a finding from the dopamine lesion experiments.

claim: Dopamine lesions primarily alter the relative levels of D1 and D2 MSN activity during two critical stages of locomotion – the initiation of movement and the performance of the gait cycle.
source: Taken together, dopamine lesions appear to primarily alter the relative levels of D1 and D2 MSN activity during two critical stages of locomotion – the initiation of movement and the performance of the gait cycle.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings from dopamine lesion experiments.

claim: Optogenetic activation of D2 MSNs reversibly altered several measures of whole-body motion.
source: Consistent with previous work (Kravitz et al., 2010), several measures of whole-body motion were reversibly altered (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: This is a finding from the optogenetic manipulation experiments supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B-E and a citation.

claim: Optogenetic activation of D2 MSNs produced significant changes in single-limb stride duration and speed, as well as more modest changes in stride length and the swing-to-stance duration ratio.
source: Concomitantly, we observed significant changes in single-limb stride duration and speed, as well as more modest changes in stride length and the swing-to-stance duration ratio (Figure 6—figure supplement 2F–I).
evidence: This is a finding from the optogenetic manipulation experiments supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2F-I.

claim: Unilaterally raising D2 MSN activity is sufficient to produce both whole-body and single-limb motor impairments with some qualitative similarities to dopamine lesions.
source: A limitation of our optical stimulation protocol is that the timing of stimulation was not phase-locked to the gait cycle; nevertheless, the results show that unilaterally raising D2 MSN activity is sufficient to produce both whole-body and single-limb motor impairments with some qualitative similarities to dopamine lesions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the optogenetic manipulation experiments.

claim: The single-limb resolution of the behavioral measurements unveiled a sizable fraction (~45%) of striatal neurons which were phase-locked to rhythmic limb movements during the gait cycle.
source: The present study investigated the electrophysiological activity of dorsal striatal neurons during self-initiated gait. The single-limb resolution of the behavioral measurements unveiled a sizable fraction (~45%) of striatal neurons which were phase-locked to rhythmic limb movements during the gait cycle.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary finding.

claim: Earlier studies have reported rhythmic firing patterns in the striatum that were attributed to single-limb motion.
source: Earlier studies have reported rhythmic firing patterns in the striatum that were attributed to single-limb motion (Rueda-Orozco and Robbe, 2015; West et al., 1990; Shi et al., 2004; Hidalgo-Balbuena et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: The study significantly expanded on prior work by quantitatively comparing the gait phase coding properties across different limbs, cell types, and dopaminergic states.
source: Here, we significantly expanded on prior work, by quantitatively comparing the gait phase coding properties across different limbs, cell types, and dopaminergic states.
evidence: This is a characterization of the study's contribution.

claim: A subset of striatal neurons represents multiple parameters involved in initiating and continuously performing walking.
source: The data suggest that a subset of striatal neurons represents multiple parameters involved in initiating and continuously performing walking, as shown by the finding of mixed coding for single-limb and whole-body motion.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The striatum may serve diverse functions required for locomotion, including the initiation of whole-body movements as well as the production or maintenance of ongoing gait at a particular speed.
source: A potential interpretation of this mixed code is that the striatum may serve diverse functions required for locomotion, including the initiation of whole-body movements as well as the production or maintenance of ongoing gait at a particular speed.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The primary motor cortex, which projects to dorsal striatum, has been shown to exhibit rhythmic spiking activity consistent with gait phase coding.
source: For example, the primary motor cortex, which projects to dorsal striatum, has been shown to exhibit rhythmic spiking activity consistent with gait phase coding (Armstrong and Drew, 1984), suggesting a shared mechanism underlying the production of this code.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: There may be a shared mechanism underlying the production of gait phase coding between motor cortex and striatum.
source: For example, the primary motor cortex, which projects to dorsal striatum, has been shown to exhibit rhythmic spiking activity consistent with gait phase coding (Armstrong and Drew, 1984), suggesting a shared mechanism underlying the production of this code.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on cited work.

claim: The findings are consistent with a large body of work demonstrating that striatal neurons encode multiple kinematic parameters including initiation, speed, and single-limb motion.
source: Our findings are consistent with a large body of work demonstrating that striatal neurons encode multiple kinematic parameters including initiation, speed, and single-limb motion (Jin and Costa, 2010; Fobbs et al., 2020; Rueda-Orozco and Robbe, 2015; Barbera et al., 2016; Gritton et al., 2019), as well as a variety of habitual behaviors and action sequences (Jog et al., 1999; Dhawale et al., 2021; Markowitz et al., 2018; Panigrahi et al., 2015; Klaus et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison of the findings to prior work with supporting citations.

claim: The most parsimonious interpretation of the data is that both discrete and continuous actions are represented in the striatum.
source: There is some disagreement about the extent to which striatal neurons represent discrete or continuous actions (e.g. initiation and cessation versus ongoing gait) (Fobbs et al., 2020; Sales-Carbonell et al., 2018). However, the most parsimonious interpretation of our and others' data is that both discrete and continuous actions are represented (Klaus et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior work with supporting citations.

claim: Behavioral studies provide evidence that striatal neurons serve a role in both initiating and maintaining locomotion and other actions.
source: Behavioral studies provide further evidence that striatal neurons serve a role in both initiating and maintaining locomotion and other actions (Tecuapetla et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Activating D1/D2 MSNs increases/decreases the frequency of initiating movement as well as the speed and duration of each walking bout.
source: For example, activating D1/D2 MSNs increases/decreases the frequency of initiating movement (a discrete event) as well as the speed and duration of each walking bout (measures of continuous motion) (Roseberry et al., 2016; Kravitz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Limb phase coding cells represented the smallest population (~45%) compared to start/stop (~90%) or speed (~90%) coding cells.
source: We found a different percentage of striatal neurons which encoded limb phase, movement initiation or cessation, and speed (Figure 3). Among these three categories, limb phase coding cells represented the smallest population with ~45% of neurons, as opposed to ~90% for start/stop or speed.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Nearly all phase coding cells were also significantly responsive to start/stop or speed, whereas a sizable proportion of start/stop or speed coding cells were not entrained to limb phase.
source: In addition, nearly all phase coding cells were also significantly responsive to start/stop or speed, whereas a sizable proportion of start/stop or speed coding cells were not entrained to limb phase.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis.

claim: The findings provide additional support to several studies demonstrating co-activation of direct and indirect pathways during movement initiation and ongoing movement.
source: On one hand, our results provide additional support to several studies demonstrating co-activation of these pathways during movement initiation and ongoing movement (Parker et al., 2018; Maltese et al., 2021; Barbera et al., 2016; Cui et al., 2013; Klaus et al., 2017; Tecuapetla et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior work with supporting citations.

claim: An imbalance in D1 versus D2 MSN activity may be important for the initial, discrete event in the movement execution sequence, but once locomotion is underway, balanced activity may be optimal for the production of the gait cycle.
source: On the other hand, the data suggest that an imbalance in D1 versus D2 MSN activity may actually be important for the initial, discrete event in the movement execution sequence, but that once locomotion is underway, balanced activity may be optimal for the production of the gait cycle.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: There is a need to distinguish between the relative activity of D1 and D2 MSNs in the 'start' and 'gait cycle maintenance' stages of locomotion.
source: Taken together, the data suggest the need to distinguish between the relative activity of D1 and D2 MSNs in the 'start' and 'gait cycle maintenance' stages of locomotion.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The significant bias toward higher D1 MSN start activity was not reported in previous studies which relied on measuring calcium dynamics.
source: The significant bias toward higher D1 MSN start activity was not reported in previous studies which relied on measuring calcium dynamics (Parker et al., 2018; Maltese et al., 2021; Barbera et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work with supporting citations.

claim: The discrepancy in D1 MSN start activity findings arose from differences in temporal resolution between single-unit electrophysiology and single-cell calcium imaging.
source: We speculate that this discrepancy arose from differences in temporal resolution between single-unit electrophysiology and single-cell calcium imaging.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the discrepancy with prior work.

claim: Both the current data and a study employing whole-cell membrane potential recordings suggest that the D1 MSN bias is only apparent in the initial stages of body or whisker movements.
source: Indeed, both our data, and a study employing whole-cell membrane potential recordings, suggest that the D1 MSN bias is only apparent in the initial stages of body or whisker movements (Sippy et al., 2015), a response that may have been missed by slower temporal resolution measurement techniques.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior work with a supporting citation.

claim: Another study employing optogenetic tagging did not find significant D1/D2 MSN differences in start/stop activity.
source: We also note that another study employing optogenetic tagging did not find significant D1/D2 MSN differences in start/stop activity (Jin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work with a supporting citation.

claim: Imbalances between D1 and D2 MSN start activity may be more pronounced under specific behavioral conditions, or results may vary depending on how movement initiation and cessation events are identified.
